title: Grandfathering existing investors indefinitely keeps the concession alive on most of the housing stock for decades
oneLiner: An argument that the bill is too timid, made from the reform side.
body: Because anyone negatively gearing before budget night keeps the concession for as long as they hold the property, the change bites only on future purchases of established homes. A government member in the House debate urged phasing out the deduction on existing properties over seven years instead.
contextBackground: Grandfathering is the price of the policy's politics: it protects every current investor. The cost is that the measured effects, on prices and on the budget, arrive slowly.
contextDisagreement: Supporters of grandfathering say retrospective change would be unfair and would trigger the forced sales the rent objection fears; critics say a dated phase-out is neither.

evidenceItems.citation: House of Representatives debate, 3 June 2026 — call for a seven-year phase-out on existing properties

otherClaim.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes

claimItself.title: Parliament should pass the 2026 budget's restriction of negative gearing to newly built homes
claimItself.oneLiner: The policy is now a bill before the Senate: negative gearing for new builds only from July 2027, existing investors grandfathered, and a reworked capital gains discount alongside it.
claimItself.body: The 12 May 2026 budget restricted negative gearing to newly built residential property for investments made after budget night, with effect from 1 July 2027, and replaced the 50 per cent capital gains discount with an inflation-based discount and a 30 per cent floor. Anyone using the concessions before budget night keeps them. A Senate inquiry took evidence in June 2026.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
